newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: EMU delay would send Portugal bond spreads soaring.
newsitem.headline: EMU delay would send Portugal bond spreads soaring.

text.p: France's pause for a rethink on a key tenet of the single currency -- the Stability Pact -- drove Portuguese bond spreads sharply wider with Bunds on Monday but it was nothing compared with what will happen if monetary union is really put in doubt, analysts said.
The yield gap in the 10-year benchmark bond jumped to 80 basis points from 74 at the opening and compared with 50 points just two and a half weeks ago.

If the market became convinced that the launch of economic and monetary union (EMU) was going to be delayed beyond its expected January 1999 start up date, the spread would quickly rise well above 100 basis points, analysts said.

Any suggestion that it was not going to happen at all, however, would send the yield gap spiralling towards 300 or 400 basis points, levels that existed before investors began to bet on Portugal and Spain making the grade for the single currency.

"As long as there is uncertainty over the euro (single currency), the market is going to be volatile and the spreads (against the Bunds) will widen," said Nuno Botelho of Banco Mello de Investimento (BMI).

The newly-elected Socialist-led government in France told its European partners at a meeting of finance ministers on Monday that it needed more time to think about the Stability Pact, one of the pillars of monetary union.

The Stability Pact commits members of the single currency to fiscal discipline once inside, with fines being imposed on those that break its rules. But the French also want commitments about economic growth and the need to promote employment.
France's Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said that his country remained fully committed to seeing the single currency launched on time.

But he added that it was unlikely that there would be any accord about the final wording of a Stability Pact ahead of the Amsterdam summit set for June 16 and 17, leaving markets plenty of time to fret.

"The volatility will remain and everybody is going to keep their eyes on France to see what their real objectives are, seeing as how Germany, despite its own problems, appears determined to press ahead with the launch date (for the euro)," said Nuno Godinho of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"If there were a delay, for example for two years, the spread (with the Bund) could go initially to 180 basis points before later adjusting over the subsequent weeks to 130 or 140," he said.
"A delay of six months would probably see an initial limit of 140 basis points before it settled around 100," he added.

Analysts said that despite Portugal's sound economic fundamentals, the key factor in the sharp narrowing with the Bunds over the past year had been confidence in the timing of the launch of the single currency,
"Under a catastrophic scenario...we could end up in a situation in which there is no euro and the spreads could widen to 300 or 400 basis points," said Miguel Pessanha, chief economist at Banco Cisf.
"But I don't believe the project (single currency) will be abandoned," he added.

Analysts said that the yields being offered on Portuguese 10-year bonds, around 6.6 percent on Monday, assumed that inflation would be held under control for the next decade, an assumption that was only valid with the single currency.
But not all analysts were so pessimistic about the impact of a delay to the single currency.
Some felt that after the initial shock had been absorbed, the market would come to see that Portugal was committed to a policy of tight fiscal currency, regardless.

"With a delay, the spreads would go above 100 basis points, but later there is no reason why they should not return to their current levels, if the project (the single currency) is not actually abandoned," said Luis Pina of Banco ESSI.
"The yields are based on good fundamentals and Portugal would continue to defend (economic) policies of convergence," he said,
--Lisbon bureau 3511-3150035
